cases.expected_outcome_notes: Deterministic: polluter sets Config.mode = 1 and never restores it; victim asserts Config.mode == 0. Victim passes alone and fails every time it runs after the polluter.

Deterministic: polluter calls System.setProperty("odfixture.turbo", "true") and never clears it; victim asserts FeatureFlags.isTurboEnabled() is false. Victim passes alone and fails every time it runs after the polluter.

Edge case for the sequence minimiser: removing either single polluter makes the victim pass again, so a one-by-one polluter search alone will not identify this case correctly. Victim fails only when both ToggleAPolluterTest#setFlagA and ToggleBPolluterTest#setFlagB have run before it; the relative order of A and B does not matter.

This is not evidence against the expected_outcome (VERIFIED) above; it is evidence the one-by-one search needs W10 (multi-polluter search) before this case can be confirmed end to end.

Deliberately fails in isolation (assertEquals(2, 1) always fails). Any tool must report this as not order-dependent because it already fails with no polluter run first. Confirmed against the finalized Phase 3 decision table (eval/outcome.py): this maps to UNRESOLVED(VICTIM_FAILS_ALONE).

Fails intermittently, independent of any shared static field, system property, or execution order. Originally guessed NOT_REPRODUCED in Phase 1 (flagged there as pending confirmation). Resolved once the Phase 3 decision table was finalized: the isolation check observes the SAME failure signature recurring at least once even when run alone with no polluter present, which trips UNRESOLVED(VICTIM_FAILS_ALONE) before reproduction counting is ever consulted -- not NOT_REPRODUCED, since it does sometimes fail, just not because of any polluter. This is the correct category for any failure that recurs by itself, deterministically (N1) or intermittently (N2).

MECHANISM FIXED 2026-10-10: originally used System.nanoTime() % 2L == 0L, which inspects nanoTime()'s lowest bit. On a real machine (Windows 11, JDK 21) that bit was always 0 (the timer's resolution was a 100ns-granular, always-even value), so the test deterministically PASSED there -- 0/40 failures, both alone and in the full order -- the opposite of 'unrelated to the environment.' On the original Linux/JDK8 container the same mechanism gave a genuine ~55-60% failure rate (12/20 in one Phase-1 measurement), so the bug was real but environment-specific, not visible everywhere. Replaced with new java.util.Random().nextBoolean(), which mixes nanoTime() with a per-call atomic counter through a full LCG rather than exposing one raw timer bit. Re-verified for real on both environments after the fix: native Windows/JDK24 11/20 fail (45%), Docker Linux/JDK8 10/20 fail (50%) -- genuinely balanced on both, confirming the fix addresses the root cause rather than just moving the symptom. See docs/evidence-m3.md for the full investigation.
